What I teach

Instruction & Services

I instruct at West Valley Flying Club (Palo Alto (PAO) and San Carlos (SQL)), and I also fly with pilots in their own aircraft. Everything below is something I actually teach. Each item names the regulation or standard behind it, so you can read the requirement yourself rather than take my word for it.

On this page

Just starting out Private Pilot certificate Instrument rating Commercial Pilot certificate Flight review Endorsements and checkouts Your own aircraft Getting back into flying

Most of my instruction is in glass-cockpit airplanes such as the Cessna 182 Skylane with the Garmin G1000. Other airplanes I instruct in are listed on the Aircraft page. How I charge, and how scheduling works, is on Rates & Policies.

Just starting out

  • Introductory flight — A ground briefing, a flight with you at the controls, and an honest conversation afterwards about what a certificate takes. No commitment beyond that one flight.
  • Student pilot — Getting you legally into the left seat: the student pilot certificate (applied for through IACRA), the medical certificate, pre-solo training and the knowledge quiz, and the endorsements you need before your first solo and your first solo cross-country. Read: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart C — especially §61.87 solo requirements and §61.93 solo cross-country.

Private Pilot certificate

From your first lesson to the checkride, in three phases: solo, solo cross-country, and practical test. What the certificate takes, how long it tends to take, and what it costs are covered in the FAQ.

  • Read: Part 61, Subpart E — §61.103 eligibility, §61.105 aeronautical knowledge, §61.107 flight proficiency, §61.109 aeronautical experience.
  • Standard: Private Pilot – Airplane Airman Certification Standards (ACS).

Instrument rating

Real-world IFR in a technically advanced airplane: procedures, decision-making and the G1000 workflow, flown to a variety of approach types at different airports rather than the same ILS every lesson.

  • Instrument rating — Read: §61.65 · Standard: Instrument Rating – Airplane ACS.
  • Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC) — When your instrument currency has lapsed beyond the grace period. Read: §61.57(d).
  • Instrument currency flights — Approaches, holds and course intercepts with a safety pilot or an instructor to stay current. Read: §61.57(c).

Commercial Pilot certificate

Tighter tolerances, smoother handling, and the maneuvers the commercial standard asks for. The certificate also lets you be paid to fly.

  • Read: Part 61, Subpart F — §61.129 aeronautical experience.
  • Standard: Commercial Pilot – Airplane ACS.

Flight review

Required every 24 calendar months: at least one hour of ground and one hour of flight. I treat it as a chance to fix habits, not a formality.

  • Read: §61.56 and AC 61-98, Currency Requirements and Guidance for the Flight Review.

Endorsements and checkouts

  • High-performance endorsement — Any airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower, which includes the Cessna 182. Read: §61.31(f).
  • Complex endorsement — Retractable gear, flaps and a controllable-pitch propeller. Read: §61.31(e).
  • Aircraft checkout — Club checkout in a make and model new to you, or a transition into the C182 and the G1000.
  • Glass-cockpit transition — Moving from a six-pack panel to the G1000: the PFD and MFD, the autopilot, and the failure modes.
  • Endorsement wording: AC 61-65, Certification: Pilots and Flight and Ground Instructors.

Your own aircraft

I am happy to fly with pilots who own or rent their own airplane: primary training, ratings, a flight review, or a checkout in a new-to-you type. Insurance requirements for owner aircraft are on Rates & Policies.

Getting back into flying

If it has been a few years, we start where you are. A flight review is usually the framework, with as much ground and air time as it takes to be safe and comfortable again. AOPA's Rusty Pilots material is a good place to start reading before we fly.
